claims.claim: Reading comprehension is an active process: readers construct meaning by posing questions, seeking answers, and clarifying confusing elements — a conversation with the text rather than passive decoding.

Readers match their approach to their purpose: skimming takes in the major points or gist of a passage, scanning locates a specific detail such as a date, name, or phrase, and close reading attends carefully to details, language, and structure.
Previewing before reading — checking titles, headings, introductory and concluding paragraphs, and other guides — helps a reader form expectations and decide how to read the text.

Paragraphs are built around a main idea: the topic sentence states in a general way what idea the paragraph deals with, supporting details develop it, and transitions and signposts link ideas between sentences and paragraphs.
Annotating and summarizing are comprehension strategies: annotations capture questions, key ideas, and reactions selectively, and a summary condenses a text's main ideas into the reader's own words.
Rereading is normal and expected in comprehension reading: reading for college is recursive, and readers return to passages to determine meaning and make connections.
Headings, subheadings, visuals, and other text features often name main ideas and serve as guides that readers can use while skimming or reading.

The belief that a reader must read every word — and that faster reading always means worse comprehension — is an attitude that limits reading flexibility; effective readers vary their pace with their purpose, and second-language readers' rates differ sharply across tasks such as scanning, skimming, and learning.

The three-part purpose framework (skim, scan, close read) is a common practical model, not a fixed taxonomy: research studies distinguish finer-grained reading tasks such as normal reading, learning, and memorizing alongside scanning and skimming.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources describe reading purposes with different granularity: some pair skimming and scanning as the two fast techniques, while reading-rate research distinguishes five tasks (scanning, skimming, normal reading, learning, memorizing).
positions: OpenStax's college-success handbook frames the choice as skimming several sources for familiarity versus reading closely for minute details.
Skimming-and-scanning training literature treats skimming for main ideas and scanning for details or specific words as the two rapid-reading techniques.
Fraser (2007) measured reading rate across five distinct tasks, showing the gap between first- and second-language rates is not the same across tasks.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents skimming, scanning, and close reading as the common three-part practical framework and notes that purposes can be finer-grained; the five-task research framing appears only in the evidence packet, not as a competing taxonomy in the lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: "Close reading" is defined differently across traditions: literary close reading develops interpretive claims about a text, while general study skills treat it as careful attention to detail.
positions: Pima Open's introduction to close reading describes it as careful, deliberate analysis that moves beyond literal summary, notices patterns, and supports an interpretation with textual examples.
OpenStax college-success materials contrast reading closely for details with skimming for familiarity.
The OpenStax Writing Guide's critical-response process separates a first reading for understanding from a second, critical reading for purpose, language, and evaluation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines close reading at the general comprehension level — careful attention to details, language, and structure — and mentions the pattern-noticing, evidence-based habit without importing genre-specific literary coursework.

sourceRecords.title: Reading Rate in L1 Mandarin Chinese and L2 English across Five Reading Tasks (EJ774867)
sourceRecords.provider: ERIC, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education (index record; article by Carol A. Fraser, 2007, peer-reviewed)
sourceRecords.notes: Record read via the ERIC API (api.ies.ed.gov, search id:EJ774867); the canonical eric.ed.gov record page is registered. Peer-reviewed study comparing first- and second-language reading rates across five tasks (scanning, skimming, normal reading, learning, memorizing); results showed substantial L1/L2 rate gaps that were not the same across tasks. Cited to support task-dependent reading rate and to frame L2 reading variation without a deficit model.
